Northern pintail (Anas acuta) females begin nesting shortly after arrival on breeding grounds, constructing shallow depressions lined with down in upland vegetation. The incubation period is closely tied to thermal conditions, and eggs maintained at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] typically hatch after approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days], though field studies report a range extending from 22 to 24 days depending on local weather and nest attentiveness. Upon hatching, precocial chicks emerge weighing around 25 grams [Wwb = around 25 grams], a modest initial mass that necessitates rapid feeding on aquatic invertebrates to fuel early growth. This neonatal body mass is among the lower values recorded for dabbling ducks of comparable adult size, reflecting the species’ strategy of producing relatively large clutches at the expense of individual egg mass. The downy young are capable of leaving the nest within hours, following the hen to productive wetland habitats where they begin exogenous feeding almost immediately.

Adult body mass in Northern pintails shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern common among anatids in which males typically outweigh females. The ultimate wet weight for females stabilizes around 680 grams [Wwi = around 680 grams], while males attain a larger asymptotic mass of approximately 730 grams [Wwi = approximately 730 grams], a difference that may reflect the energetic demands of male aerial displays and territory defence during the breeding season. These mass values are derived from measurements of wintering and pre-breeding individuals in good body condition, with some regional variation linked to latitude and habitat quality. The comparatively slender build of the pintail relative to other Anas species is thought to enhance flight efficiency during long-distance migrations, which for this species can exceed several thousand kilometres between Arctic breeding grounds and temperate or tropical wintering sites. Body condition at the onset of spring migration is a key predictor of subsequent reproductive success.

The timing of developmental milestones in Northern pintails is best understood under the thermoneutral conditions characteristic of the active metabolic period in adult waterfowl, approximately 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, fledging—the achievement of sustained flight—occurs at 46 days after hatching [tx = 46 days after hatching], a relatively rapid transition for a long-distance migrant that requires well-developed flight muscles before autumn departure at a temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. Sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to breed, is reached approximately 70 days after hatching [tp = approximately 70 days after hatching], although most individuals do not actually attempt nesting until their first or second year due to the need to acquire breeding experience and establi at a temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]sh territories. This interval between fledging and puberty represents a period of continued somatic development and foraging skill acquisition.

Reproductive effort in Northern pintails is concentrated into a single annual cycle, reflecting the short Arctic summer during which most breeding occurs. Females typically produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], with each clutch containing 7 to 9 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 7 to 9 eggs], a combination that yields a moderate annual reproductive output for a dabbling duck. The first successful breeding event is typically deferred until one year after hatching, such that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days] when measured under the same thermoneutral conditions of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. This age at first reproduction is typical for medium-sized waterfowl and allows for a full year of somatic growth and behavioural maturation before the energetic demands of nesting and brood-rearing are undertaken. Clutch size can vary with female age and nutritional status.

Longevity in Northern pintails is constrained by the hazards of migration and predation, though the species exhibits a life span comparable to that of other migratory dabbling ducks. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild, derived from banding returns, is approximately 10,001 days [am = approximately 10,001 days] when evaluated under the thermoneutral conditions of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C] that represent active metabolic life. This exceptional lifespan places the pintail among the longer-lived members of the genus Anas, with only a small fraction of individuals surviving to such advanced ages. Most mortality occurs during the first year of life, driven by predation on ducklings and the challenges of initial migration. Adult annual survival rates in well-studied populations are estimated at 60 to 70 percent, figures that underscore the importance of high fecundity in compensating for extensive juvenile losses.
